answer_text:
Let

\[
f(z)=\sum_{n=4}^{\infty} a_n z^n
\]

since \(f\) has a zero of order \(4\) at \(0\). We want to bound \(a_4=f^{(4)}(0)/4!\).

Define the successive quotients

\[
f_0(z)=f(z),\qquad f_{j+1}(z)=\frac{f_j(z)}{z}\quad (j=0,1,2,3),
\]

where the removable singularity at \(z=0\) is filled in by the value \(f_j'(0)\). Because \(f\) has a zero of order \(4\), each of \(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3\) also vanishes at \(0\).

Now apply Schwarz’s lemma iteratively.

- Since \(|f_0(z)|\le 1\) and \(f_0(0)=0\), Schwarz’s lemma gives

\[
|f_0(z)|\le |z|.
\]

- Hence \(f_1(z)=f_0(z)/z\) is holomorphic on the unit disk, satisfies \(|f_1(z)|\le 1\), and \(f_1(0)=0\). Again by Schwarz’s lemma,

\[
|f_1(z)|\le |z|.
\]

Repeating this four times gives

\[
|f_3(z)|\le |z|.
\]

Therefore

\[
f_4(z)=\frac{f(z)}{z^4}
\]

is holomorphic on the unit disk and satisfies

\[
|f_4(z)|\le 1.
\]

But

\[
f_4(0)=a_4=\frac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}.
\]

Thus

\[
|a_4|\le 1,
\]

so

\[
|f^{(4)}(0)|=4!|a_4|\le 24.
\]

The value \(24\) is attained, for example, by \(f(z)=z^4\), since \(|z^4|\le 1\) on the unit disk and

\[
(f(z))^{(4)}(0)=24.
\]

To characterize equality, suppose

\[
|f^{(4)}(0)|=24.
\]

Then \(|f_4(0)|=1\). Since \(f_4\) is holomorphic and bounded by \(1\) on the unit disk, the maximum modulus principle forces \(f_4\) to be constant of modulus \(1\). Hence

\[
f_4(z)=e^{i\theta}
\]

for some real \(\theta\), and therefore

\[
f(z)=e^{i\theta}z^4.
\]

Conversely, every function of the form \(f(z)=e^{i\theta}z^4\) satisfies all the hypotheses and gives

\[
|f^{(4)}(0)|=24.
\]

Thus the maximum is

\[
\boxed{24\text{, attained exactly by }f(z)=e^{i\theta}z^4\text{ with }\theta\in\mathbb{R}.}
\]

27B·v4.method: Iterative application of Schwarz lemma to successive quotients f/z^j to show f/z^4 is bounded by 1, then maximum modulus for equality.
